title: A token is not a word.
lede: Models read tokens, not English. Byte-pair encoding splits rare strings into pieces: ‘unhappiness’ might be un, happiness. ‘🚀’ can be several tokens. The bill and the window (plate 253) are in tokens. A tokenizer is part of the model; mix them and you lie.
diagram: Left: 4 words. Right: 7 tokens — ‘ChatGPT’ 2–3 tokens, ‘undefined’ maybe 1, a UUID many. Caption: tiktoken / sentencepiece. Count before you ship a 12k-word paste.
what: Subword units from a fixed vocab. Encode on the way in, decode on the way out. Whitespace and code tokenize densely.
why: ‘The model ignored the end of my prompt’ is often a window in tokens, not words. Also: cost.
trap: Splitting on spaces and calling it tokens. Using GPT-4’s tokenizer to budget a Llama. Assuming 1 token ≈ 1 word (rule of thumb 0.75 words, not a law).

title: The window is a token budget.
lede: The context window is prompt tokens + generated tokens, together, not ‘the file size.’ Overflow is drop or refuse — the model does not silently remember the head (plate 12, 21). Long context is slower and dearer: attention is still paid per token, even with tricks.
diagram: 1 window 128k. 2 system 2k + RAG 20k + chat 10k = 32k in. 3 max_out 4k. 4 room left 92k. Caption: output eats the same budget. A 100k paste + 8k answer needs 108k.
what: One integer: n_in + n_out ≤ window. Reserve output. Position 0 is not free; some models weaken in the middle.
why: RAG stuffing and ‘just put the repo in the prompt.’ Count, don’t guess (plate 252).
trap: Measuring characters. Ignoring output. Assuming 1M context is free and accurate at every offset.

title: KV cache is the past, paid once.
lede: For each new token, attention needs keys and values of all previous tokens. The KV cache stores them so you do not recompute the prefix. Prefill builds the cache (prompt). Decode reads it and appends one token. That is why the first token is slow and the rest are cheaper (plate 266).
diagram: Left (bad): re-embed the whole prompt every output token — n² waste. Right (hit): prefill once → cache; each decode step is 1 vs n. Caption: cache size ≈ layers × n_tokens × d × 2. Long chats eat GPU RAM, not just the window.
what: Memoized attention state. Prefix reuse is also prompt caching (plate 265) across requests.
why: Streaming, chat, and why batching decode is a different game from prefill.
trap: Changing a system prompt at token 0 invalidates the whole cache. Thinking the cache is ‘memory’ the model understands — it is math, not a diary (plate 12).

title: Chunk so retrieval can hit.
lede: RAG retrieves pieces, not books (plate 21). Chunk too big: the embedding is mush and you waste the window. Too small: a sentence without its antecedent. Overlap so a split sentence still lands in one hit. The chunk is the unit of truth you will cite (plate 270).
diagram: 1 512–1024 tokens, 10–20% overlap. 2 store {text, loc, id}. 3 retrieve k, stuff, answer. Caption: split on headings/paragraphs before tokens. Tables: keep a row together. Code: by function, not by 500 chars mid-line.
what: Chunking is the index schema. Retrieval can only return what you stored. Metadata (title, date) filters before cosine.
why: ‘RAG is dumb’ is often chunking. Interview: size, overlap, and what you embed (question vs hypothetical).
trap: One embedding per PDF. Sliding 50-token windows with no overlap. Embedding the question in a different model than the chunks.

title: Words, or meaning. Then both.
lede: BM25 (and inverted indexes, plate 217) match terms: exact SKUs, error codes, names. Embeddings match meaning (plate 22): ‘how do I reset my passcode’ ≈ ‘forgot password.’ Neither wins always. Hybrid is the default: lexical + vector, then fuse.
diagram: Left: query ‘ORD-1840’ — BM25 hits, embedding may miss. Right: query ‘make it stop charging twice’ — embedding hits ‘duplicate payment’, BM25 may not. Caption: keyword filter then vector, or RRF merge of two ranked lists (plate 257).
what: Sparse vs dense retrieval. Use both when the corpus has IDs and prose. Language of the query should match the embedder.
why: Search + RAG design. Interviews love ‘why not only vectors.’
trap: Embeddings-only on a parts catalog. BM25-only on paraphrased support tickets. Embedding with model A, querying with model B.

title: Hybrid retrieves. A reranker sorts.
lede: Retrieve broadly (BM25 ∪ vectors, k=50), then a reranker (plate 258) scores the query against each candidate and keeps 5. First stage is recall; second is precision. Stuffing 50 chunks into the window is not ranking — it is hoping (plate 253).
diagram: 1 hybrid retrieve 50. 2 cross-encoder scores pairs. 3 top 5 + citations into the prompt. Caption: Reciprocal Rank Fusion merges two lists without calibrated scores. Dedup near-duplicate chunks before the model.
what: Two-stage retrieval. Cheap wide, expensive narrow. The generator never sees the junk if you cut.
why: Production RAG. ‘We retrieve 20’ is a smell unless you rerank.
trap: k=3 from a single vector store and calling it done. Reranking 500 on every keystroke. No citation map from the 5 back to the 50.

title: A reranker is a second, smaller model.
lede: A bi-encoder embeds query and doc separately (fast, cacheable). A cross-encoder reads (query, doc) together and outputs a relevance score — slower, sharper. That second model is the reranker. It does not retrieve; it sorts what you already have.
diagram: Left: cosine(q, d) from two vectors — cheap, approximate. Right (hit): model([q; d]) → score. 50 pairs, not 1e6. Caption: distilled rerankers (miniLM) are the usual. The LLM itself can rerank, at 10× cost.
what: Pairwise relevance. Use on a shortlist. Cache nothing about the pair except the score for that query.
why: The missing piece after ‘we did embeddings.’ SDE-2 GenAI.
trap: Cross-encoding the whole corpus. Using the generator as the only ranker with a 20k prompt. A reranker trained on news applied to code.

title: RAG fails at the chunk, not the prose.
lede: Hallucination after RAG is often a retrieval miss, a stale chunk, or two chunks that disagree — then the model reconciles in a fluent lie (plate 45). Debug the index before the prompt. If the right paragraph never entered the window, no temperature will save you (plate 44).
diagram: Box1 Miss — query ≠ chunk language; hybrid (plate 256). Box2 Stale — doc updated, index not. Box3 Conflict — policy v3 and v1 both retrieved; cite dates. Caption: eval retrieval separately: recall@k, then answer quality (plate 262).
what: Failure modes: miss, junk, stale, conflict, citation gap. The generator is last.
why: ‘Just add RAG’ postmortems. Interviews: how you know it retrieved the right thing.
trap: Only reading the final sentence. Re-chunking in the prompt instead of the index. Never checking the retrieved set when the answer is wrong.

title: Structured output is a schema, not a plea.
lede: ‘Reply in JSON’ is a hope. Constrained decoding / tool schemas make illegal tokens unrepresentable. Validate with a real JSON Schema (or Zod) after, because even constrained models can pass a schema and fail your semantics. Retry on fail; don’t regex a maybe.
diagram: Left (bad): prompt ‘return JSON’ → {"ok": maybe trailing prose. Right (hit): response_format json_schema / tool parameters; parse; if invalid, repair once. Caption: enums in the schema beat ‘one of red, green’ in English.
what: Grammar on the tokens + validator on the value. Tools (plate 47) are schemas with side effects.
why: Anything you will pipe to a DB or a function. Interviews: why the prompt is not the contract.
trap: eval() on model JSON. No schema, then split on the first { . Asking for JSON and markdown in the same breath.

title: An agent is a loop of tools.
lede: An agent is not a smarter model. It is a loop: model → tool call (plate 47) → observation → model, until it stops or you kill it. Bound the steps, the tools, and the blast radius (plate 272). Logs are the product.
diagram: 1 user. 2 model: tool search(q). 3 you run search, return hits. 4 model: tool click(id) or final answer. Stop at N=8. Caption: ReAct is this with thoughts. Multi-agent is extra loops and extra failure.
what: LLM + tools + a termination condition. State is the message list. You execute tools, not the model.
why: ‘Should we build an agent?’ Only if the task is multi-step and tool-shaped. Otherwise RAG or one tool call.
trap: Unbounded loops. Tools that can DELETE. No idempotency on tool side (plate 225). Calling it autonomous when it is a for-loop.

title: Evals are a golden set, not a vibe.
lede: You cannot ship a prompt change on ‘it felt better.’ A frozen set of (input, acceptable output / facts) scored by code, retrieval metrics, and maybe a judge (plate 263). Run on every prompt and model bump. Online metrics (thumbs, cost) are extra, not instead.
diagram: 1 100 cases: question, must-include facts, forbidden. 2 retrieve recall@k. 3 answer exact / contains / JSON valid. 4 fail the build if recall drops. Caption: version the set. Slice by topic. A/B is not an eval of correctness.
what: Regression tests for models. Separate retrieval eval from generation eval (plate 259).
why: The difference between a demo and a system. SDE-2 GenAI expects this sentence.
trap: Tuning on the eval set until it is a training set. One-number ‘accuracy’ on free prose. Changing the judge and the prompt in the same PR.

title: A judge model has a bias too.
lede: LLM-as-judge: another model grades the answer. It is noisy, position-biased (prefers the first), and length-biased (prefers longer). Use it when code cannot score. Calibrate against humans on a slice. Swap order; average. Prefer checklists (‘contains X’) over 1–5 stars.
diagram: Left: ‘score 1-5 which is better, A or B’ — A always listed first wins. Right (hit): rubric of binary facts; swap A/B; two judges. Caption: do not use the same model as generator and only judge.
what: A noisy metric. Good for ranking prompts, bad as the only ship gate. Human spot-check stays.
why: Evals at scale. Interviews: limits of judges.
trap: Letting the judge see the gold and the model’s chain-of-thought and calling it blind. One call, one number, ship.

title: Guardrails wrap the model.
lede: The model is not your policy engine. Filter input (PII, injection — plate 46), constrain tools, filter output (toxicity, secrets, schema). Fail closed on payments and PII; fail open on a copy tweak. Logs of blocks are how you debug without leaking (plate 271).
diagram: 1 inbound classify / redact. 2 model + tools with allowlist. 3 outbound regex + classifier + schema. 4 if trip: canned refusal, don’t retry into the leak. Caption: system prompt is not a guardrail. An attacker reads it.
what: Layers around the LLM. Least privilege on tools (plate 261). Same as authZ (plate 14): the model is untrusted.
why: Production LLM. Prompt injection exists; wrap anyway.
trap: ‘The system prompt says be safe.’ Outputting the user’s secrets in the refusal. Running the filter with the same untrusted tools.

title: Prompt cache is prefix reuse.
lede: If the first N tokens are identical across requests, a provider can reuse the KV (plate 254) and charge less / return faster. The prefix must be byte-stable: same system prompt, same tool schemas, same RAG header. Put the volatile user question at the end.
diagram: Left (bad): timestamp in the system prompt — prefix never hits. Right (hit): [static tools + policy][docs][user]. Caption: a one-token change at position 0 misses. Some APIs need a minimum prefix length.
what: Cache the stable head. Dynamic content goes last. This is not RAG cache (doc embeddings).
why: Cost and TTFT on a busy copilot. Same reason CDNs like immutable URLs.
trap: ISO timestamps and request ids in the system message. Reordering tools every call. Caching a prefix that includes the user’s PII.

title: TTFT is wait. TPS is the stream.
lede: Time to first token is prefill: eat the prompt, build KV (plate 254). Tokens per second is decode: one token at a time. Users feel TTFT as ‘is it broken?’ and TPS as ‘is it typing.’ A huge prompt wrecks TTFT even if TPS looks fine. Stream; don’t buffer the essay.
diagram: Left: 8s silence then a dump — no stream. Right: 0.4s TTFT, then 40 tok/s. Caption: batching helps TPS, can hurt TTFT. Streaming is HTTP chunked / SSE, not a spinner.
what: Two metrics, two stages. Optimize prompt size for TTFT; batching and smaller models for TPS.
why: UX and capacity planning. ‘The model is slow’ is which one?
trap: Reporting only average latency of the full answer. A 100k prefix and wondering why the first token took 12s. Buffering until JSON is complete when the user wanted tokens.

title: Batch the cheap calls.
lede: Embeddings and classification love batches: one kernel, many inputs. Generative decode is pickier (different lengths, KV). Offline: batch 32–256. Online: a tiny window (10–50ms) to group arrivals without adding a beat to TTFT.
diagram: Left: 1000 embed HTTP calls. Right: one POST with 1000 strings. Caption: same model, same tokenizer. Pad to the longest in the batch — huge pads waste. Sort by length.
what: Throughput vs latency. Batch what is embarrassingly parallel. Don’t batch interactive chat across users if it delays first token.
why: Ingest pipelines, evals, backfills. Cost graphs that look like a sawtooth of 1-QPS.
trap: Batching 1. Padding a 4-token query to 8k. Mixing models in one batch.

title: LoRA is a small delta, not a new brain.
lede: Fine-tune (plate 48) can be full weights or LoRA: small rank adapters on attention/MLP. You teach style, format, a dialect — not facts that change weekly (that is RAG) and not a one-off instruction (that is a prompt). Serving: load adapters, don’t duplicate the base.
diagram: Box1 Prompt — new instruction. Box2 RAG — new documents. Box3 LoRA — new behavior burned in. Caption: if you can retrieve it, don’t train it. If you need JSON every time, a schema (plate 260) may beat a tune.
what: Low-rank update. Base model stays. Many adapters on one base. Eval still required (plate 262).
why: The third option in prompt/RAG/tune, with the cost in the right bucket.
trap: Fine-tuning on facts that will go stale. One full 70B copy per customer. Calling LoRA ‘a new model’ in capacity math without the base.

title: Pixels arrive as tokens too.
lede: A vision model tiles the image into patches and embeds them as tokens in the same window (plate 253). A 4k screenshot can be thousands of tokens — more than the caption. Resolution and tile count are the budget. Audio is chunks of spectrogram, same idea.
diagram: 1 image 1024² → N tiles. 2 each tile ~ tokens. 3 plus your text. Caption: ‘look at the screenshot’ can blow the window before the question. Downscale UI shots; crop the table.
what: Multimodal = extra tokens with a spatial layout. They compete with text in the same budget.
why: Copilots that ‘see’ the IDE. Cost surprises.
trap: Sending a 12MP photo for a 20-word answer. Assuming the model reads tiny 6px font in a full-page screenshot. Ignoring that tiles can drop the corners you cared about.

title: Cite it, or it didn't happen.
lede: Ungrounded fluent answers are hallucinations with better manners (plate 45). Require chunk ids (plate 255) in the schema (plate 260). Highlight the span. If the model cannot point, it must say it doesn’t know. Citations you don’t verify are theater.
diagram: Left: ‘according to policy…’ no link. Right: answer + [{id: 'p12', quote: '…'}] — UI links to p12. Reject if id not in retrieved set. Caption: the model can invent ids. Check membership.
what: Grounding = retrieve, constrain, verify. The citation is data, not prose.
why: Support, legal, medical-adjacent, internal docs. Trust is the product.
trap: Footnotes the model invented. Citing the filename but not the chunk. Showing five docs and answering from none of them.

title: PII in the prompt is PII in the logs.
lede: Whatever you send to the model is copied: provider logs, your traces, the GPU cache, the eval dump. Redact before the call. Minimize retention. Don’t paste a spreadsheet ‘for context.’ Training-on-your-data is a contract, not a vibe.
diagram: 1 detect SSN/email/card. 2 replace with tokens [EMAIL_1]. 3 call model. 4 map back in your app, never in the provider. Caption: screenshots (plate 269) are PII too. Prompt cache (plate 265) may store the prefix — don’t put secrets there.
what: Treat the LLM like a third-party HTTP API (plate 9). DLP on the way out. Access control on traces.
why: Enterprise GenAI. The leak is usually logs, not the weights.
trap: Sending prod DB rows to a playground key. Logging full prompts in Datadog at 15-day retention. Masking in the UI and not in the API.

title: Text-to-SQL has a blast radius.
lede: A model that writes SQL is a user with your DBA’s vocabulary and a stranger’s intent. Allow SELECT on views, not DROP. Parameterize (plate 16). Limit rows. Dry-run EXPLAIN (plate 98). The schema you stuff is a leak and an injection surface (plate 46).
diagram: Left (bad): execute whatever string the model returns as the DB role. Right (hit): allowlist tables; parse AST; reject writes; timeout; row cap; audit. Caption: a tool (plate 47) with a read replica (plate 37). Never the primary with migrations.
what: LLM proposes, policy executes. Least privilege. Idempotent reads.
why: Internal copilots. The outage is one generated JOIN.
trap: Admin connection string. ‘The prompt says only SELECT.’ Concatenating user text into the SQL the model already wrote.

title: Tokens are the bill.
lede: You pay for input tokens and, usually more per token, output. Cached prefixes (plate 265) are cheaper. A 40k RAG dump on every chat turn is a product decision with a unit cost. Trace cost per feature, not one OpenAI invoice.
diagram: Box1 input $ — prompt + tools + RAG. Box2 output $ — long answers, retries, agents (N loops). Box3 cache hit. Caption: an agent of 8 steps is ~8× a single call (plate 261). Evals have a bill too.
what: Unit economics = tokens × price × retries. Shrink retrieval, cap max_out, cache the prefix, don’t loop unbound.
why: The feature that was ‘just an LLM call’ at 10 users. SDE-2: how you would cap it.
trap: Ignoring output tokens. Retry storms. Logging 100k-token traces at full fidelity to a paid APM.
